# Laos warty newt

Laos Warty Newt

The Laos warty newt (Laotriton laoensis), also known as the Laotian crocodile newt, is a species of salamander in the family Salamandridae. It is found only in the Saysomboun Special Zone and Phou Kout District in Xiangkhouang Province, Laos. It is considered one of the rarest newts in the world and as of 2014, has been classified as endangered due to its restricted geographic range and ongoing habitat loss.
Description
The Laos warty newt is a relatively large newt species for this region, typically measuring between 15 and 20 centimeters in length and weighing approximately 20-35 grams. It is characterized by rough, warty skin that gives it a crocodile-like appearance, which is the origin for its common name. These individuals are generally brown in color, often marked with red and orange patterns.
Distribution
Its natural habitats are subtropical or tropical dry shrubland and rivers. This species is native to the mountain regions of Southeast Asia, where it inhabits elevations ranging from about 1,200 to 1,800 meters above sea level. These salamanders are more commonly found in cool, damp environments. The Laos warty newt prefers temperatures between 15 and 22 degrees C and relies on shaded, humid conditions to maintain its moisture levels.
Behavior and Ecology
The Laos warty newt is usually nocturnal, remaining hidden during the day beneath stones, leaves, and other sheltered locations to avoid heat and remain cool. However, they may occasionally be active during daylight hours following rainfall.
Diet
This salamander's diet consists of mainly small invertebrates found both on land and in aquatic environments. Common prey can include insects, worms, larvae, small snails, freshwater shrimp, and mosquito larvae.
Reproduction
Relatively little is known about the reproductive biology of this species in the wild. Breeding is believed to occur during the rainy season, typically between the months of May and August. Females are though to lay eggs individually or in small groups near streams, where larvae develop in water over a period of several months.
Conservation status
Sometimes this newt is classified as Paramesotriton laoensis. Since 1999, the population of this newt in the wild has been decimated by wildlife trading networks. The Laos warty newt is considered endangered due to its limited distribution and ongoing degradation of its natural habitat. Its rarity and environmental requirements make it particularly vulnerable to environmental changes, including deforestation and habitat disturbance.
Lifespan
In the wild, the Laos warty newt is estimated to have a lifespan of approximately 10 to 15 years.
